Give them faithful witnesses, and make me willing to speak and serve when You give opportunity. Teach me to pray with love, patience, and perseverance. Amen.

phase_title: Learning How to Serve and Reproduce
title: Praying for Opportunities
lesson:
Paul asks believers to pray that God would open a door for the word so that he could speak the mystery of Christ clearly. Remarkably, he writes this while imprisoned. His concern is not merely for an open prison door but an open gospel door.

This teaches us to pray specifically for opportunities.

An open door may be a question, a crisis, a conversation during work, a neighbor's curiosity, an invitation, or simply enough trust in a relationship to speak honestly about faith.

Paul also asks for clarity. Opportunity alone is not enough; we need wisdom to make the message understandable.

Praying for open doors changes how we move through the day. Instead of assuming spiritual conversations must be manufactured, we begin watching for opportunities God may already be providing.

Not every conversation must become a full gospel presentation. Sometimes one honest sentence prepares the way for another conversation later.

Pray for the door, pray for clarity, and remain attentive enough to notice when the door opens.
what_this_means: Evangelistic opportunities are not limited to special church events. God can open doors inside ordinary relationships and ordinary days.
heart_question: If you prayed every morning for one gospel opportunity, what situations during your normal week might you begin noticing differently?
practical_assignment: For the next seven mornings, ask God for one open door and clarity to use it. Each evening, write whether you noticed any spiritual opening.
prayer: Father, open doors for Your Word in the ordinary places I go. Make me attentive enough to notice them and courageous enough to enter them wisely. Give me clear words about Christ and protect me from forcing conversations You have not opened. Use even small moments to move people toward truth. Amen.

phase_title: Learning How to Serve and Reproduce
title: Depending on the Holy Spirit
lesson:
Before sending the disciples outward as witnesses, Jesus told them to wait for the promised Holy Spirit. They were not to attempt the mission merely through personality, training, or determination.

Jesus said they would receive power when the Holy Spirit came upon them and would be His witnesses from Jerusalem outward to the ends of the earth.

The book of Acts records a unique redemptive-historical transition as the risen Christ establishes His church and the gospel spreads. We should respect that context rather than treating every event in Acts as a formula to reproduce mechanically. Yet the enduring truth is clear: Christian witness depends upon God's Spirit.

Dependence does not mean lack of preparation. The Spirit can use Scripture we have learned, testimony we have prepared, and thoughtful answers we have studied. Dependence means we know technique cannot create spiritual life.

Pray before conversations. Ask for courage, wisdom, love, and clarity. Trust God to work in ways you cannot see.

Your responsibility is faithful witness. The Spirit's work in another person's heart is not yours to control.
what_this_means: You can prepare carefully without believing conversion depends upon your skill. Witness faithfully and depend upon God's Spirit for what only God can do.
heart_question: Do you feel personally responsible for making someone believe, or have you learned to distinguish your responsibility from the Holy Spirit's work?
practical_assignment: Before your next spiritual conversation, pray specifically for the Spirit's help. Afterwards, evaluate your faithfulness rather than trying to measure whether you controlled the outcome.
prayer: Holy Spirit, empower me to bear faithful witness to Jesus Christ. Give me courage, love, wisdom, and clarity. Keep me from trusting techniques or believing I can produce spiritual life in another person. Use the truth of Your Word and help me leave results in God's hands. Amen.

phase_title: Learning How to Serve and Reproduce
title: Inviting Someone to Respond to Christ
lesson:
The Philippian jailer asked Paul and Silas, “What must I do to be saved?” Their answer directed him to the Lord Jesus: “Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ.”

The passage then says they spoke the word of the Lord to him and his household. This reminds us not to reduce evangelism to getting someone to repeat a sentence without understanding the gospel. The jailer received instruction and responded with faith and visible change.

When sharing Christ, it is appropriate to invite a response. You might ask, “What is keeping you from trusting Christ?” or “Do you understand what it means to turn to God and rely upon Jesus?”

Avoid manipulation. Emotional pressure, misleading promises, or declaring someone converted merely because they repeated words can create false assurance. Prayer does not save; Christ saves. A prayer can express repentance and faith when it genuinely reflects the heart.

Also do not be afraid to ask a clear question. Endless conversation that never calls for response can leave the gospel abstract.

Explain Christ faithfully, invite the person to respond, and entrust the heart to God.
what_this_means: A gospel conversation may appropriately call for a decision, but your goal is genuine repentance and faith in Christ, not merely obtaining a verbal response.
heart_question: Are you more likely to pressure someone for an immediate response or avoid ever asking them what they will do with the gospel?
practical_assignment: Practice three respectful questions that invite a person to respond to Christ without manipulation or promises you cannot make.
prayer: Lord Jesus, help me present Your gospel clearly and invite people to respond without pressure or fear. Protect me from confusing repeated words with saving faith. Give me discernment, courage, and patience, and let those who hear truly understand and rely upon You. Amen.

phase_title: Learning How to Serve and Reproduce
title: Helping a New Believer Begin
lesson:
After Peter preached Christ, his hearers were cut to the heart and asked what they should do. The response included repentance and baptism, and those who received the word were added to the community. They then continued in the apostles' doctrine, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayers.

Conversion is a beginning, not a graduation.

When someone professes faith in Christ, do not simply celebrate and disappear. Help that person begin learning Scripture, praying, connecting with a sound local church, understanding baptism, and developing relationships with mature believers.

Avoid creating dependence upon yourself. You may be one helper, but the new believer needs the wider body of Christ and trustworthy leadership.

Also avoid overwhelming someone with dozens of rules. Begin with the gospel and the basic practices Scripture emphasizes.

Ask questions about understanding. New believers may carry assumptions from previous religion, culture, or media that need patient biblical correction.

The goal is not merely to count a decision. It is to help a new disciple take the first faithful steps of following Jesus.
what_this_means: If God allows you to lead someone toward Christ, your concern should extend beyond the moment of profession toward that person's growth in a local church and God's Word.
heart_question: If someone trusted Christ through a conversation with you today, would you know the first few steps to help that person begin growing?
practical_assignment: Write a simple first-week plan for a new believer: one Gospel passage to read, one prayer practice, one church connection, and one follow-up conversation.
prayer: Father, help me care about disciples, not merely decisions. If You allow me to help someone come to Christ, give me patience to encourage the first steps of growth. Lead that person into Your Word, prayer, baptism, healthy fellowship, and faithful church life. Keep me from making anyone dependent upon me instead of Christ. Amen.

phase_title: Learning How to Serve and Reproduce
title: Teaching Someone Else
lesson:
Paul tells Timothy to be strong in the grace found in Christ and to entrust what he has heard to faithful people who will be able to teach others also.

Four generations are visible: Paul, Timothy, faithful people, and others. Biblical discipleship is designed to multiply.

Notice what is passed on: trustworthy teaching. Reproduction is not merely duplicating our personality, preferences, or traditions. We want people to know Scripture and follow Christ.

The people Timothy chooses should also be faithful and able to teach. Character and reliability matter alongside knowledge.

You may feel unqualified to disciple anyone because you still have much to learn. You do not need to know everything before helping someone with what you understand. At the same time, stay humble, remain teachable, and do not teach beyond your knowledge.

Discipling someone can be simple: read Scripture together, discuss meaning and application, pray, answer questions, model Christian life, and encourage involvement in church.

What you receive should not stop with you.

A mature disciple increasingly asks, “Whom can I help take the next step?”
what_this_means: You can remain a learner while helping another person learn. Discipleship multiplies when truth is faithfully passed from one person to another.
heart_question: Who is one person you may be able to help grow spiritually without pretending to be an expert?
practical_assignment: Invite one younger or newer believer to read a short Bible passage with you regularly for the next four weeks. Keep the meeting simple and Scripture-centered.
prayer: Father, thank You for people who have taught me Your truth. Help me receive it faithfully and pass it on without adding my pride or preferences. Show me someone I can encourage, give me humility to keep learning, and make me dependable in helping others follow Christ. Amen.

phase_title: Learning How to Serve and Reproduce
title: Making Disciples, Not Just Converts
lesson:
Jesus begins the Great Commission with His authority: all authority in heaven and earth belongs to Him. On that basis He commands His followers to make disciples of all nations.

The commission includes going, baptizing, and teaching people to observe everything Christ commanded. Evangelism is therefore essential but not isolated from discipleship. The goal is not merely a moment of agreement; it is people becoming followers of Jesus.

Baptism publicly identifies the disciple with the Triune God, and teaching continues throughout Christian life. Notice that Jesus says to teach obedience, not merely information.

The mission reaches all nations. The church's concern cannot remain confined to people who are culturally familiar or geographically close.

Yet the command ends with comfort: “I am with you always.” The One who sends His church does not abandon it.

Your role in the Great Commission may include personal witness, discipling another believer, praying, giving, sending, serving through a local church, or crossing cultures with the gospel.

Every Christian should locate his or her life somewhere inside Christ's mission.
what_this_means: Jesus did not command His church merely to collect professions of faith. He commands us to make disciples who are baptized, taught, and learning obedience.
heart_question: Where does your present life connect practically with Christ's command to make disciples?
practical_assignment: Write one action you can take in each area: pray, witness, strengthen another believer, and support gospel work beyond your immediate circle. Begin one this week.
prayer: Lord Jesus, all authority belongs to You. Give me a life that participates in Your command to make disciples. Help me share the gospel, value baptism and teaching, encourage obedience, and care about the nations. Thank You that You do not send Your people alone but promise Your presence with them. Amen.

phase_title: Learning How to Serve and Reproduce
title: Your Mission Field Starts Where You Are
lesson:
Jesus told His disciples they would be witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and to the end of the earth. Acts then traces the gospel moving outward across geographic and cultural boundaries.

The verse is not a rigid formula requiring every Christian to reproduce those exact locations. It reveals a mission that begins where the disciples are and expands beyond familiar boundaries.

Your “Jerusalem” includes people already around you—family, neighbors, coworkers, classmates, customers, and friends. It is possible to become fascinated with distant mission while remaining silent with people we see every week.

But the verse also prevents local concern from becoming the limit. God's heart reaches nations and people unlike us. Every church should care about gospel advance beyond its own community.

Some believers will cross cultures personally. Others will pray, give, encourage missionaries, welcome outsiders, or help send people.

Do not wait for an exotic opportunity before becoming a witness. Faithfulness begins where your feet already are and remains willing to go wherever Christ opens the way.
what_this_means: Your everyday relationships are already part of the mission field, while Christ also calls His church to look beyond its own community toward the nations.
heart_question: Who are the people in your normal weekly life who currently have the clearest opportunity to observe and hear your Christian witness?
practical_assignment: Draw four circles: Home, Community, Nation, World. Put names or ministries in each circle and choose one practical mission action for the coming month.
prayer: Lord Jesus, make me faithful where I already am and willing to look beyond what is familiar. Give me courage to witness to people near me and a heart for people and nations beyond my immediate world. Show me how to pray, give, go, welcome, and speak as part of Your mission. Amen.

phase_title: Learning How to Serve and Reproduce
title: A Disciple Who Makes Disciples
lesson:
At the beginning of Jesus' ministry, He called fishermen with the words, “Follow Me, and I will make you fishers of men.” They left their nets and followed Him.

Those words summarize the journey you have been taking. A disciple follows Jesus. Christ changes the disciple. And the changed disciple becomes involved in reaching others.

Following comes first. We cannot lead people where we refuse to go ourselves. Continue learning Scripture, praying, participating in the local church, confessing sin, obeying Christ, and depending upon His grace.

“I will make you” reminds us that growth is Christ's work in us. Ninety lessons do not produce a finished Christian. Discipleship lasts a lifetime.

“Fishers of men” turns the disciple outward. What you have received is meant to bless others. Serve. Share the gospel. Encourage younger believers. Teach what you know faithfully. Keep learning while helping someone else learn.

This is not the end of your discipleship path. It is a transition from being intentionally established in the basics toward a lifetime of following and reproducing.

Keep following Jesus—and help someone else follow Him too.
what_this_means: The goal of this ninety-day journey is not a certificate of spiritual completion. It is a stable beginning: following Christ personally and becoming useful in helping others follow Him.
heart_question: After ninety days, what is your clearest next step in following Jesus, and who might God be calling you to encourage or disciple?
practical_assignment: Create a 90-day continuation plan with four commitments: personal Bible and prayer, local church involvement, one area of service, and one person for whom you will pray and intentionally encourage toward Christ.
prayer: Lord Jesus, thank You for calling me to follow You. Continue changing me through Your Word, Your Spirit, and Your church. Keep me humble, teachable, obedient, and dependent upon grace. Make me useful in serving others, courageous in sharing the gospel, and faithful in helping others become disciples. I want to keep following You for the rest of my life. Amen.
